opus-5.5.text:
I think the analogy to Cursor is useful, but it also shows where math is different.

What made Cursor work wasn't only a better model. It fit into an existing workflow. Programmers already lived in an editor, already had a compiler, tests, and version control. The AI just slotted into the loop: you write, it suggests, you run it, you see whether it works. That feedback loop already existed, and the product made it faster.

In mathematics, that loop has historically been missing. When a mathematician writes a proof, the "compiler" is another human being: a referee, a colleague, sometimes a whole community spending months or years checking it. So if you just put a language model next to a mathematician and have it generate informal proofs, you get something that sounds very convincing and may be subtly wrong. Everyone has seen this. The model produces a beautiful-looking argument with a gap in step seven, and checking it costs the human more time than writing it themselves.

So for me, the Cursor moment in math has to be built on verification. That's why formal languages like Lean matter so much. A proof in Lean is checked by the machine. It either compiles or it doesn't. That gives you the equivalent of the compiler and the test suite. Once you have that, AI can explore, propose lemmas, try strategies, fail many times, and only bring back what actually checks. The human stops being a proofreader and goes back to being the person with taste: deciding which questions matter, which definitions are natural, which direction is worth exploring.

As a product, I think about it in layers. The first layer is autoformalization: taking math as humans actually write it, in papers and on blackboards, and turning it into formal statements and proofs. That's the bridge, because most mathematicians don't write Lean today and shouldn't have to. The second layer is the prover: given a formal statement, find a proof, or find a counterexample. The third layer, the most exciting and the hardest, is conjecturing: the system notices patterns and proposes statements worth proving. Discovery, not just verification.

The real breakthrough happens when these layers connect smoothly enough that a working mathematician feels it the way a programmer felt Cursor: "I can't go back." Not because it's flashy, but because it removes drudgery and gives you trust. You can say, "This lemma is fine, the machine checked it," and spend your attention on the deep idea.

There's also a bigger picture beyond professional mathematicians. Math is the language underneath chip design, cryptography, software verification, and a lot of engineering where correctness really matters. If you have an AI that reasons rigorously and whose outputs come with a guarantee, that's valuable far beyond pure math. So I see mathematics as both the product and the proving ground. It's the cleanest environment we have for building AI that doesn't just sound right but is right.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't have that product yet, and the reason is instructive.

Cursor worked because code has a tight feedback loop. You write something, you run it, it either compiles or it doesn't, the tests pass or they don't. The model gets signal constantly, and the human gets signal constantly. Math research doesn't look like that for most working mathematicians. You can spend three weeks on an idea and the only feedback is a vague feeling that it's not going anywhere. So the first question for a "Cursor for math" is: where does the signal come from?

That's really why I care so much about formalization. Lean gives you the compiler. Once a statement and a proof live in a formal system, you have the same binary check that software engineers take for granted. It's not that mathematicians will all suddenly want to write Lean. Most of them won't, and they shouldn't have to. But if the system underneath is formal, then the AI can be wrong a thousand times in the background and only surface the things that actually verify. That changes the trust relationship completely. With a chatbot, every claim is something I have to check myself, which for a hard proof is often more work than doing it from scratch. With a verified system, I can actually delegate.

So the product shape I imagine is something like this. The mathematician still owns the question and the intuition, the high-level architecture of the argument. The model handles the enormous search space underneath: trying lemmas, finding counterexamples, checking that the thing you believe is true in case n=3 is actually true in general. The interaction should feel like working with a very fast, very stubborn postdoc who never gets tired and never lies to you about whether something is proven.

The part people underestimate is that "autocomplete" is the wrong metaphor. In coding, the next token is often locally predictable. In math, the interesting moves are precisely the ones that aren't locally predictable, where you pull in an idea from a completely different area. So the breakthrough isn't going to be a faster way to type what you already know. It's a system that can go away for hours, explore, and come back with something you didn't see, with a proof certificate attached so you don't have to take its word for it.

And then there's the question of who it's for. Cursor's user base was tens of millions of developers. Research mathematicians are maybe tens of thousands. If you build only for them, it's a wonderful thing but not a company. I think the actual market is everyone who needs rigorous reasoning and currently can't afford it: engineers verifying hardware, people writing safety-critical software, finance, eventually anyone who wants a guarantee rather than a plausible-sounding answer. Math is the hardest version of that problem, so if you solve it there, the rest comes along. That's the bet.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is: what would make a mathematician want to use this every day? A Cursor-like breakthrough would have to fit into the way people actually do mathematics, where you’re exploring examples, trying a conjecture, getting stuck, and changing your approach.

So I’d be excited about something that lets you say, “Here’s what I’m thinking. Can you find a counterexample? Is there a simpler case I should look at? Where does this argument break?” Those are useful interactions even before the system can independently solve a hard research problem.

And there’s a real trust issue. If it gives you a plausible-looking proof with a subtle mistake, you can spend more time debugging it than you saved. The product needs to make its reasoning inspectable and, where possible, verifiable.

For me, the breakthrough would be when that loop becomes so useful and so easy that you naturally keep it open while you work. That’s a different milestone from getting an impressive answer to a benchmark problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to ask what the mathematician is actually doing all day. Writing a proof is part of it, but you’re also trying examples, looking for counterexamples, reading papers, and figuring out whether two things that look different are actually connected. A really useful product would help you move between those activities without losing the context of the problem.

The analogy to Cursor is that it meets you where you already work. For mathematics, I’d want something where I can share an incomplete argument and say, “This step feels wrong. Can we test it?” Maybe the right next action is a computation, maybe it’s finding a relevant theorem, or maybe it’s formalizing a small piece so we can check it precisely.

The hard part is trust. A plausible-looking proof can waste a lot of time if there’s a subtle mistake. So the product has to make clear what has been verified, what depends on an assumption, and what is still a guess.

To me, the breakthrough would be when mathematicians keep it open because it consistently helps them get unstuck. Solving a difficult problem once is exciting. Helping someone make progress every day is what makes it a product.
